canonical_name: Weisfeiler-Leman graph-isomorphism heuristic/refinement family (exact proposition open)
literal_source_claim_en: A heuristic algorithm for graph isomorphism.
source_attribution: Weisfeiler/Lehman, 1968 (catalog metadata only; no work, edition, theorem, section, or page is cited)
statement_blocker: The catalog supplies only an algorithm-family label and the gloss 'a heuristic algorithm for graph isomorphism'. It does not select the original ordered-arc/coherent-closure procedure, modern 1-WL vertex color refinement, k-WL tuple refinement, or another variant; nor does it select invariance, sound rejection, stabilization, complexity, class-specific completeness, a limitation, or a counterexample as the theorem. It fixes no graph model, colors, update, stopping rule, output, cost model, ordered binders, hypotheses, conclusion, or boundary cases. Generic graph-isomorphism completeness would be a false substitution: the inspected 2018 preface says the original completeness conjectures were incorrect.
target_decision: redirect the catalog algorithm-family gloss to one corrected, independently reviewed, immutable-source proposition before statement or proof execution
domain_and_universes: Open: an approved source must fix the graph representation and vertex universes, simple/directed/colored/labeled/looped/multigraph conventions, finiteness and decidability context, algorithm variant and dimension, color carrier and initialization, refinement update and color-renaming semantics, comparison and stopping rule, output, cost and computation model, and all typeclass context.
conclusion: Open: the repository does not choose well-definedness, isomorphism invariance, sound rejection, stabilization, a runtime bound, class-specific completeness, coherent-closure correctness, a limitation, a counterexample, or another proposition.
degenerate_case_status: No case is excluded at intake because no proposition is selected; the statement phase must resolve empty and singleton graphs, unequal vertex counts, zero rounds or dimension, initial-color and stable-partition edge cases, loops/directions/multiplicity/labels, separate versus disjoint-union comparison, indistinguishable nonisomorphic graphs, malformed encodings, hash collisions, and small-input cost conventions.
